Repeat tasks when possible to account for variation.

A practical comparison table could look like this:

MetricWhat it tells youTask completion rateWhether the agent finishes useful workTest pass rateWhether the result meets defined checksRegression rateWhether changes break existing behaviorHuman correction timeHow much engineering effort remainsEnd-to-end latencyHow long delivery takesCost per accepted changeWhether the workflow is economically usefulPolicy complianceWhether the agent respects project restrictions

The important distinction is between a model that generates a plausible answer and a system that consistently produces accepted engineering work.

6. The future belongs to complete engineering systems, not isolated models

Kimi K3.1 Pro illustrates three directions in AI development.

First, models are being optimized for longer, more complex tasks rather than just short prompts.

Second, the systems around models are becoming more important. Tool execution, delegation, resource budgets, retries, and verification influence whether model capability translates into practical productivity.

Third, open-weight releases force a more explicit discussion of the trade-off between access, customization, and control.

The launch-related quota problems are especially instructive. Strong benchmark results do not guarantee that a service will provide a smooth experience under real usage. A capable model still needs reliable infrastructure and sensible resource management.

That is not unique to Kimi. Every AI coding platform faces some version of this challenge as it moves from demonstrations to sustained engineering work.

For developers, the strategic question is therefore not simply, “Which model is smartest?”

It is:

Which model, toolchain, and verification process can deliver the highest rate of correct, maintainable software within our cost and security constraints?

That is a more demanding question, but it is also the one that matters in production.

Final thought

Kimi K3.1 Pro is an important release to watch. Its reported coding performance puts it close to leading proprietary models on a notable agent benchmark, while its planned open-weight release could give developers more deployment flexibility.

But the early launch experience shows why model intelligence alone is not enough. Agent orchestration must control unnecessary work, infrastructure must handle demand, and security safeguards must account for the capabilities being released.

The next generation of AI coding tools will not win solely by generating better code.

They will win by turning model capability into reliable, secure, cost-effective engineering outcomes.

Would you choose an open-weight coding model with more control over deployment, or a hosted model with a more mature managed experience? What would determine your decision?

medium.titulo: I Let AI Write 100% of My Code for 30 Days. Here’s What Broke.
medium.resumo: I want to be precise about what I did, because the phrase “AI wrote my code” has been diluted into meaninglessness. I don’t mean copilot…
medium.conteudo_html:
I want to be precise about what I did, because the phrase “AI wrote my code” has been diluted into meaninglessness. I don’t mean copilot suggestions I tidied up. I don’t mean a function here and there. I made a rule and held it for thirty days: I do not type application code. The AI does. My job is to describe, to review, and to approve — and if I ever reached into the editor to fix something myself, that counted as a failure I had to write down.

I shipped a real product this way. A small SaaS with authentication, Stripe billing, a dashboard, and a public API. It works, it’s in production, and people are paying for it. Somewhere in those thirty days I stopped wondering whether the machine could write code and started learning something more interesting: exactly where the “AI writes everything now” story holds together, and exactly where it quietly comes apart in your hands.

This is not a hype post and it is not a doom post. It’s a field report from someone who took the premise as literally as it would go.

## The rules I held myself to

The exercise only means anything if the rules are strict, so they were. I didn’t write application logic by hand — I prompted, and the AI wrote. I let myself read every line, reject it, and ask again, but I couldn’t open the file and fix it myself. Config, secrets, and “go click this button in the dashboard” steps stayed mine, mostly because the AI can’t do them anyway. And the one escape hatch: if I got genuinely stuck for more than an hour, I logged it as a “break” and wrote the code myself.

By the end I had nine logged breaks. Everything worth saying lives in those breaks — but first I owe the machine honesty about how much it got right.

## What worked, and it worked shockingly well

Greenfield scaffolding is, as far as I can tell, a solved problem. “Set up a Next.js app with Postgres, Drizzle, and auth” produced a correct, coherent starting point in one shot, and the first forty percent of the project flew by faster than I have ever built anything. Boilerplate it simply does not get wrong — CRUD endpoints, Zod schemas, a table with sorting and pagination came out clean every time. And as a thinking partner it’s remarkable: I asked why a query was slow and it spotted a missing index and an N+1 in the same breath. For that first week I was half-drafting the “developers are obsolete” post in my head.

Then week two arrived and started charging rent.

## What broke: the nine breaks, honestly

The first three breaks were the same disease wearing different clothes. The AI is brilliant at the file in front of it and blind to the one three folders over. A second `formatCurrency` helper because it didn’t know the first existed. My auth check re-implemented inline instead of the middleware already sitting there. A subtly different `User` type in a new module. None of these were bugs — everything compiled, everything passed. They were architecture drift, invisible right up until the day it costs you a week. The model optimizes locally and beautifully; holding a whole system coherent is still a human job, and it turns out to be most of the job.

Breaks four and five were scarier, because they weren’t crashes. The billing webhook the AI wrote acknowledged Stripe events before persisting them. In testing it was flawless. In production, one database blip leaves you with a paying customer who has no access and no record they ever paid — a support nightmare that surfaces days later with no trail. I only caught it because I’ve been burned by that exact shape before. A junior copying this output, trusting it because it ran and looked right, would have shipped it. The failure wasn’t in the syntax; it was in a decision, and the decision looked identical to a correct one.

Break six was the loop of despair. Asking the AI to fix what it couldn’t see produced changes, not fixes — it rewrote the function, assured me the bug was gone, and reintroduced it two prompts later. Debugging a system through the same model that wrote it is a hall of mirrors. Without dropping into a debugger myself to understand the real state, we would have spun forever.

Breaks seven and eight were about taste, which the AI has none of. Ask for a settings page and it hands you fourteen options no user requested. Ask for error handling and it swallows every error whole. Its instinct is always to add; it cannot say “no, less.” Knowing what to leave out is a huge, unglamorous fraction of engineering, and it’s a judgment the model simply does not possess.

And break nine: the last ten percent was ninety percent of the month. “Demo works” took a week; “handles a real user doing something weird at 2am” took the other three. Edge cases, race conditions, the empty state, the error state, the double-click state — none of it happens unless you know to ask, and knowing to ask is the whole job.

## The uncomfortable synthesis

Here’s what I actually believe after thirty days. AI didn’t replace me — it replaced the tasks I used to hand to juniors. The scaffolding, the boilerplate, the first draft: the exact work a junior becomes a senior by doing. So where does the next senior come from? You can’t skip the ten thousand hours; you can only move where they’re spent. The skills that mattered every day were senior ones — knowing the code was subtly wrong, knowing what not to build, holding the whole system in my head. AI didn’t flatten the hierarchy. It made the top more valuable and sawed off the ladder to reach it.

## What I changed

I didn’t stop using AI — I use it for one hundred percent of the typing now and always will. I changed the guardrails. The thing that writes the code is never the thing that reviews it: a separate reviewer, prompted to refute the diff, catches the plausible-but-wrong code the author always waves through. Nothing merges without a human who can see the blast radius the model can’t. “It compiles and the tests pass” is the start of review, not the end — because the model writes tests that agree with its own wrong mental model.

Author here, skeptic there, human on the merge button. That separation is the whole reason I could hand the typing to a machine and still sleep. It’s also exactly how we build [xenition](https://xenition.com): agents that do the work, a different agent that tries to tear it down, and a person who owns the decision.

## Would I do it again?

For a prototype, in a heartbeat — I’d never scaffold by hand again. For production, I’ll use AI for one hundred percent of the typing and zero percent of the thinking. The typing was never the hard part. It just felt like it was.

On 22 October, Anthropic donated Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation, the Linux Foundation project that already hosts MCP and AGENTS.md. According to Anthropic’s announcement, more than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and VS Code, have integrated the standard since it was published in December 2025.

For you as a developer, nothing breaks. The format stays the same, the spec still lives at agentskills.io, and you can keep using it without joining anything. What changes is the case for learning it: a skill you write today is no longer tied to one vendor’s roadmap.

So let’s write one. This article walks through a small, real skill from empty folder to “it fires when I ask for it”, using only what the spec and the Claude Code docs actually say.

What a skill is, in one paragraph

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file inside. The file has YAML frontmatter (at minimum a name and a description) followed by Markdown instructions. The folder can also hold scripts/, references/ and assets/. Agents load skills through what the spec calls progressive disclosure: at startup they read only the name and description of every skill (the spec estimates about 100 tokens each), they load the full body only when a task matches, and they open bundled files only when the instructions call for them.

That last point is the whole trick. You can keep dozens of skills installed because each one costs you a line in the listing until it’s needed. It also means one field does most of the work, and we’ll get to it in step 3.

Step 1: Pick a task worth a skill

Good first skills share three traits:

  • You do the task often enough that re-explaining it is annoying.
  • It has steps or conventions the model can’t guess (your team’s format, your tools, your order of operations).
  • You can tell whether the result is right.

Bad first skills are vague (“be a better coder”) or one-off. For this walkthrough we’ll build pr-description: a skill that turns the current branch's changes into a pull request description in a fixed format. Most teams have a format, and most agents don't know it.

Step 2: Create the folder and get the name right

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/pr-description

That path is Claude Code’s personal location, available in all your projects. For a skill your whole team should get, use .claude/skills/pr-description/ inside the repository and commit it. Other agents read skills from their own locations, so check your tool's docs for the exact path; the folder and file format are the same.

The spec is strict about name:

  • 1 to 64 characters
  • lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only
  • no leading or trailing hyphen, no --
  • it must match the folder name

pr-description passes. PR-Description and pr--description don't.

Step 3: Write the description first

The description is what the agent reads when deciding whether your skill is relevant. If it doesn’t match how you actually phrase requests, the skill never loads, and the instructions you carefully wrote never get read.

The spec gives a clear contrast. A poor description:

description: Helps with PDFs.

A good one says what the skill does and when to use it, with the keywords a user would say:

description: Extracts text and tables from PDF files, fills PDF forms, and merges multiple PDFs. Use when working with PDF documents or when the user mentions PDFs, forms, or document extraction.

A few rules that come straight from the docs:

  • Length. The spec caps description at 1,024 characters. Claude Code also truncates each skill's listing text at 1,536 characters and, when you have many skills, drops descriptions of the least-used ones to fit a budget. Put the main use case first.
  • Point of view. Anthropic’s skill authoring best practices say to write descriptions in the third person (“Writes…”, not “I can help you…”), because the text is injected into the system prompt.
  • Real phrases. Think about the three or four ways you’d actually ask: “write the PR description”, “summarize this branch for review”, “draft a pull request”.

Here’s ours:

description: Writes a pull request description from the current branch's changes, using the team template (summary, changes, testing, risks). Use when the user asks for a PR description, a pull request summary, or wants to open a PR.

Step 4: Write a short, specific body

The body has no required format. The spec recommends step-by-step instructions, examples of inputs and outputs, and common edge cases, and suggests keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines, moving long reference material into separate files. The Claude Code docs add a practical reason to stay brief: once a skill loads, its content stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring cost.

The complete file, saved as ~/.claude/skills/pr-description/SKILL.md:

---
name: pr-description
description: Writes a pull request description from the current branch's changes, using the team template (summary, changes, testing, risks). Use when the user asks for a PR description, a pull request summary, or wants to open a PR.
---

# PR description

## Steps
1. Run `git log --oneline main..HEAD` and `git diff main...HEAD --stat` to see what changed.
2. Read the diff of the files that changed most.
3. Fill in the template below. Keep each section short.
4. If the branch has no commits ahead of main, say so and stop.

## Template
### Summary
One or two sentences: what this PR does and why.

### Changes
- Bullet per meaningful change, grouped by area.

### Testing
How it was tested. If no tests were added, write "No new tests" and say why.

### Risks
Anything a reviewer should look at closely: migrations, config changes, removed code, public API changes. Write "None found" only if you checked.

## Rules
- Do not invent test results. Only report tests you ran or that exist in the diff.
- Do not mention files that did not change.

Notice what’s in there: the exact commands, the exact template, the edge case (no commits) and two rules that stop the most common failure (made-up test results). Notice what isn’t: background on why PR descriptions matter. The model doesn’t need persuading.

Step 5: Test that it fires

Claude Code watches the skills folders, so a new or edited SKILL.md is picked up in the current session without a restart. Then test it two ways, as the docs suggest:

  1. Let the agent choose it. In a repo with a feature branch, ask something that matches the description: “Can you write the PR description for this branch?”
  2. Call it directly. Type /pr-description.

If the direct call works but the natural request doesn’t, the problem is almost always the description. The Claude Code troubleshooting list for a skill that isn’t triggering is short and worth following in order:

  • Check the description includes keywords you’d naturally say.
  • Ask “What skills are available?” and confirm it’s listed.
  • Rephrase your request closer to the description.
  • If the YAML frontmatter is malformed, Claude Code still loads the body but with empty metadata, so /pr-description works while automatic matching can't. Run with --debug to see the parse error.

If it fires too often instead, make the description more specific, or add disable-model-invocation: true to the frontmatter so it only runs when you call it.

To check the file against the spec itself, the Agent Skills project provides a reference validator, skills-ref:

skills-ref validate ~/.claude/skills/pr-description

Before you install someone else’s skill

Writing your own skills is the safe part. Installing other people’s needs more care, because a skill is instructions plus, often, code your agent will run. Anthropic’s Agent Skills overview puts it plainly: use skills only from trusted sources, and audit anything from an unknown source before use. Its checklist, in short:

  • Read every file, not just SKILL.md: scripts, images, other resources.
  • Look for things that don’t match the stated purpose: unexpected network calls, unusual file access.
  • Be wary of skills that fetch from external URLs, since fetched content can carry malicious instructions, and a trustworthy skill can change if its dependencies do.
  • Remember skills can call tools. Know what your agent is allowed to run before a skill runs it.

Also note that the spec’s allowed-tools field, which pre-approves tools for a skill, is marked experimental and support varies between agents. The foundation's proposed roadmap includes security guidance for people who write and install skills, so expect this area to get more formal.

Checklist

  1. Pick a repeated task with conventions the model can’t guess.
  2. Name the folder and the skill identically: lowercase, hyphens, 64 characters max.
  3. Write the description first: what it does, then when to use it, in the words you’d actually type.
  4. Keep the body to steps, a template or example, edge cases and a few hard rules.
  5. Test both ways: a natural request and the direct /name call.
  6. If it doesn’t trigger, fix the description before touching the body.
  7. Audit every file of a third-party skill before installing it.

Where to go next

If you want all of this on a few pages you can keep open while you write, the free AI Agent Skills Quick-Start Cheat Sheet covers the format, a copy-and-adapt SKILL.md template, why most skills never trigger (with a checklist), and how to install and test skills across the major agents, in 6 pages.

When you’re ready to go further, AI Agent Skills: The Complete SKILL.md Standard Guide spends 49 pages on the full specification, five build walkthroughs from markdown-only to Python to API-calling skills, ten production-ready templates, a chapter on skills security and a 30-day plan for building a personal skills library.

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the author.

medium.conteudo_html:
A practical guide to HTTP requests, TanStack Query, error handling, and server-side rendering

When building a Vue or Nuxt application, making an HTTP request is rarely the difficult part. The real challenge is keeping API calls consistent as the application grows.

You need to handle authentication, HTTP errors, request cancellation, loading states, caching, and server-side rendering. Before long, your project has multiple API utilities, duplicated interceptors, and slightly different error-handling logic across components.

Nuxt provides $fetch and useFetch, while Vue developers can also use Axios, ofetch, or the native Fetch API. These are all useful tools, but when your application uses TanStack Query, you may want a transport layer designed specifically for its query-function contract.

That’s where tanstack-fetch comes in.

In this tutorial, we’ll build a reusable API client for Vue 3 and Nuxt, connect it to TanStack Query, and explore when this approach makes sense.

1. Understanding the problem

Consider a typical API request using Axios:

const response = await axios.get<User[]>('/api/users')
return response.data

Axios returns a response object, so we need to extract response.data. We also need to ensure that HTTP errors are handled consistently and that requests can be cancelled when they are no longer needed.

Now consider a TanStack Query query function:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['users'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    const response = await axios.get<User[]>('/api/users')
    return response.data
  },
})

This works, but every query function may need to account for the HTTP client’s response structure, error behavior, and cancellation mechanism.

As the project grows, the same concerns tend to appear in many places.

A better approach is to separate responsibilities:

  • HTTP client: Sends requests and handles transport-level behavior.
  • TanStack Query: Manages caching, retries, server state, and query lifecycle.
  • Vue or Nuxt: Renders the UI and manages application-level concerns.

The goal isn’t to replace TanStack Query. It’s to give it a cleaner HTTP client to work with.

2. What is tanstack-fetch?

tanstack-fetch is an open-source, TypeScript-first HTTP client created by Mohammad Garmabi. It is designed around the way TanStack Query expects query functions to behave.

It is an independent package, not an official TanStack project.

Its core contract is simple:

  1. Return parsed data when a request succeeds.
  2. Throw a typed FetchError when an HTTP request fails.
  3. Honor AbortSignal so requests can be cancelled.
  4. Keep authentication, interceptors, and other transport concerns in a reusable client.

For Vue and Nuxt, the package also provides optional integration helpers through tanstack-fetch/vue.

This means you can use the same underlying HTTP client without tying your API layer to a particular UI framework.

Documentation: https://mohamadgarmabi.github.io/tanstack-fetch/guide/vue

3. Installing the dependencies

For a Vue 3 application, install the client and Vue integration:

npm install tanstack-fetch vue

If you also want caching and server-state management with TanStack Query, install Vue Query:

npm install @tanstack/vue-query

For a Nuxt application, the client can be installed with:

npm install tanstack-fetch

Add @tanstack/vue-query if you plan to use TanStack Query.

One important distinction: tanstack-fetch and TanStack Query solve different problems. The first handles HTTP transport; the second manages server state.

4. Creating a reusable API client in Vue

Let’s start with a simple Vue 3 application.

Instead of creating a new HTTP client inside every component, we’ll create one shared instance.

Create src/lib/api.ts:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'
export interface User {
  id: string
  name: string
  email: string
}
export const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
})

Define the API URL in your .env file:

VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com

Now the application has one place to configure its HTTP client.

You can add authentication, status handlers, and plugins as your requirements evolve, instead of distributing those concerns across individual requests.

Connecting the client to Vue

The Vue integration provides createFetchPlugin and a useFetch composable.

In src/main.ts:

import { createApp } from 'vue'
import { createFetchPlugin } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
import { api } from './lib/api'
import App from './App.vue'
createApp(App)
  .use(createFetchPlugin({ client: api }))
  .mount('#app')

The client is now available through the Vue integration.

Inside a component:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { useFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
const api = useFetch()
const users = await api.get<User[]>('/users', {})
</script>

For applications that need shared request caching, however, we’ll usually let TanStack Query manage the request lifecycle.

5. Integrating tanstack-fetch with TanStack Query

This is where the client becomes especially useful.

Install Vue Query if you haven’t already:

npm install @tanstack/vue-query

Register its plugin in your Vue application:

import { createApp } from 'vue'
import { QueryClient, VueQueryPlugin } from '@tanstack/vue-query'
import { createFetchPlugin } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
import { api } from './lib/api'
import App from './App.vue'
const queryClient = new QueryClient()
const app = createApp(App)
app.use(VueQueryPlugin, { queryClient })
app.use(createFetchPlugin({ client: api }))
app.mount('#app')

Now create a component that fetches users.

<script setup lang="ts">
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/vue-query'
import { useFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
import type { User } from '@/lib/api'
const api = useFetch()
const {
  data: users,
  error,
  isPending,
  isError,
} = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['users'],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
    api.get<User[]>('/users', { signal }),
})
</script>
<template>
  <p v-if="isPending">Loading users...</p>
  <p v-else-if="isError">
    Failed to load users: {{ error.message }}
  </p>
  <ul v-else>
    <li v-for="user in users" :key="user.id">
      {{ user.name }} — {{ user.email }}
    </li>
  </ul>
</template>

Let’s look at the important parts.

The query key

queryKey: ['users']

TanStack Query uses this key to identify and cache the query.

The query function

queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
  api.get<User[]>('/users', { signal })

The HTTP client returns the parsed response data directly, so there is no need to unwrap an Axios response object.

Request cancellation

TanStack Query provides an AbortSignal to the query function. Passing it to api.get allows the HTTP request to participate in Query's cancellation lifecycle.

This matters when a query becomes obsolete or is cancelled during navigation or other application interactions.

Error handling

When the request fails with an HTTP error, tanstack-fetch throws a FetchError. TanStack Query can then expose the failure through its normal error state.

The result is a clear separation of responsibilities: the HTTP client handles the request, and TanStack Query manages the server state.

6. Using mutations to create data

The same approach works for POST requests.

Suppose we want to create a user and refresh the cached user list after a successful response.

<script setup lang="ts">
import {
  useMutation,
  useQueryClient,
} from '@tanstack/vue-query'
import { useFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
import type { User } from '@/lib/api'
const api = useFetch()
const queryClient = useQueryClient()
interface CreateUserInput {
  name: string
  email: string
}
const createUser = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (body: CreateUserInput) =>
    api.post<User>('/users', { body }),
  onSuccess: () => {
    void queryClient.invalidateQueries({
      queryKey: ['users'],
    })
  },
})
</script>
<template>
  <button
    :disabled="createUser.isPending.value"
    @click="
      createUser.mutate({
        name: 'Ada Lovelace',
        email: 'ada@example.com',
      })
    "
  >
    Create user
  </button>
  <p v-if="createUser.isError.value">
    {{ createUser.error.value.message }}
  </p>
</template>

This example focuses on the API integration. In a production component, the input values would normally come from a form with validation.

The key idea is that mutations use the same API client as queries. You don’t need a separate HTTP implementation for writes.

7. Setting up tanstack-fetch in Nuxt

Nuxt introduces another concern: the same application code may run on the server and in the browser.

Nuxt already provides $fetch and useFetch, so why introduce another client?

The answer depends on your architecture.

If you only need straightforward requests in Nuxt pages, the built-in tools may be sufficient. But if you want a shared HTTP client for TanStack Query, consistent typed HTTP errors, or features such as authenticated server-sent events, tanstack-fetch offers another option.

Let’s register a shared client through a Nuxt plugin.

Create plugins/tanstack-fetch.ts:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch/sse'
import { createFetchPlugin } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
export default defineNuxtPlugin((nuxtApp) => {
  const config = useRuntimeConfig()
  const api = createFetch({
    baseUrl: config.public.apiBase,
  })
  nuxtApp.vueApp.use(
    createFetchPlugin({ client: api }),
  )
  return {
    provide: {
      api,
    },
  }
})

Add the public API URL to nuxt.config.ts:

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  runtimeConfig: {
    public: {
      apiBase: 'https://api.example.com',
    },
  },
})

The plugin registers the Vue integration and exposes the client through Nuxt’s application context.

The example imports from tanstack-fetch/sse because that entry point also supports server-sent events. If you only need HTTP requests, use the core entry point instead:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'

Accessing the client in a Nuxt page

You can access the injected client through useNuxtApp():

<script setup lang="ts">
import type { User } from '@/lib/api'
const { $api } = useNuxtApp()
const users = await $api.get<User[]>('/users', {})
</script>

For a Nuxt application using TanStack Query, you can instead access the Vue composable:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/vue-query'
import { useFetch as useFetchClient } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'
interface User {
  id: string
  name: string
}
const api = useFetchClient()
const { data: users, isPending } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['users'],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
    api.get<User[]>('/users', { signal }),
})
</script>
<template>
  <p v-if="isPending">Loading...</p>
  <ul v-else>
    <li v-for="user in users" :key="user.id">
      {{ user.name }}
    </li>
  </ul>
</template>

Notice the alias:

import { useFetch as useFetchClient } from 'tanstack-fetch/vue'

Nuxt already has a composable named useFetch. Renaming the import avoids confusing Nuxt's built-in data-fetching composable with the tanstack-fetch client composable.

8. What about authentication and HTTP errors?

Real applications need more than successful GET requests.

Imagine an API that returns:

  • 401 Unauthorized when the access token is invalid.
  • 403 Forbidden when the current user lacks permission.
  • 404 Not Found when a resource does not exist.
  • 429 Too Many Requests when a rate limit is reached.
  • 500 Internal Server Error when the server encounters a problem.

You can configure status handlers on the shared client rather than duplicating the same logic in every query function.

For example:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch'
const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com',
  onUnauthorized: () => {
    // Trigger your application's authentication flow.
  },
  onForbidden: ({ status }) => {
    console.warn('Access denied:', status)
  },
  onNotFound: ({ status }) => {
    console.warn('Resource not found:', status)
  },
})

These handlers are illustrative: connect them to your actual authentication and notification systems.

One security detail is important: a 403 response should not automatically be treated as an expired session. A user may be authenticated but lack permission to access a resource. Keep authorization failures distinct from authentication failures.

If your application uses refresh tokens, configure the appropriate refresh-token interceptor rather than implementing refresh logic independently in every component.

Also remember that a shared client does not replace server-side authorization. The backend must enforce permissions on every protected endpoint.

9. Server-side rendering and cookies in Nuxt

SSR is one of the most important architectural differences between Vue SPA development and Nuxt.

During server rendering, the browser’s cookies are not automatically available to outgoing API requests. If the API relies on session cookies, your server-side client may need to forward the relevant incoming request headers.

tanstack-fetch provides an ssr-forward plugin for this use case.

The general setup involves:

  1. Reading the relevant incoming request headers on the server.
  2. Forwarding the required cookies or authorization headers to the upstream API.
  3. Avoiding unnecessary forwarding in browser-side requests.
  4. Ensuring that each server request uses the correct user’s authentication context.

For example, the configuration can use the relevant plugin:

import { createFetch } from 'tanstack-fetch/plugins'
const api = createFetch({
  baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com',
  plugins: ['ssr-forward'],
})

Treat this as an illustration of the plugin entry point, not a complete Nuxt SSR configuration. Actual header forwarding must be wired to the incoming Nuxt request using the documented SSR integration.

See the official SSR guide for the Nuxt-specific setup.

Important: Never forward all incoming headers indiscriminately, expose private credentials through runtimeConfig.public, or store user-specific authentication state in a process-wide singleton. Incorrect SSR authentication can leak data between users.

For a complete Nuxt application, configure Vue Query’s server-side prefetching and hydration separately as well. Registering an HTTP client alone does not automatically dehydrate and hydrate the query cache.

10. When should you use tanstack-fetch instead of $fetch?

Nuxt’s built-in $fetch is a good choice for server routes, simple API calls, and applications that don't need a separate transport layer.

tanstack-fetch becomes more interesting when your application needs a consistent HTTP contract across several parts of the stack.

RequirementPractical choiceSimple request in a Nuxt server route$fetchNuxt page data without TanStack QueryuseFetch or $fetchTanStack Query with a shared typed HTTP clienttanstack-fetchConsistent HTTP errors and status handlerstanstack-fetchShared transport configuration across Vue and other frameworkstanstack-fetchAuthenticated SSE with reconnection supporttanstack-fetch SSE integration

The important point isn’t that one client is universally better. Each solves a slightly different problem.

If your project is small and $fetch already meets your requirements, adding another abstraction may not be worthwhile.

If your project relies heavily on TanStack Query and needs consistent authentication, error handling, cancellation, and transport configuration, a dedicated client can reduce repeated glue code.

11. Final thoughts

A maintainable frontend architecture doesn’t require the largest possible set of abstractions. It requires clear boundaries between responsibilities.

TanStack Query should manage server state. Vue and Nuxt should handle rendering and framework-specific behavior. The HTTP client should provide a predictable interface for communicating with the backend.

tanstack-fetch is designed to connect those layers with a small, typed API that works with Vue 3 and Nuxt.

Start with a single shared client, connect it to your queries, and add authentication, SSR forwarding, or SSE only when your application needs them.

You can explore the package, examples, and framework integrations here:

  • Documentation: https://mohamadgarmabi.github.io/tanstack-fetch/
  • Vue & Nuxt guide: https://mohamadgarmabi.github.io/tanstack-fetch/guide/vue
  • TanStack Query integration: https://mohamadgarmabi.github.io/tanstack-fetch/guide/tanstack-query
  • GitHub: https://github.com/mohamadgarmabi/tanstack-fetch

The objective is straightforward: fewer duplicated transport concerns, predictable errors, and a cleaner boundary between HTTP requests and server-state management.

What I learned building Unframed: one set of components for React, Vue, Angular and plain HTML, on web standards. And the problems that turned out to be the interesting part.

Most companies don’t have one frontend. They have a React app, an Angular admin panel that’s been around for years, a Vue project someone started for a campaign, and a few plain HTML pages. And each of them gets its own buttons, inputs, dialogs and date pickers.

That means the same design is rebuilt three or four times. Every fix has to be made three or four times. Every accessibility bug gets solved in one place and lives on in the others. Over time the “same” button drifts into four slightly different buttons.

I wanted to see how far I could get with the opposite approach: build the components once, on web standards, and make them feel native in every framework. The result is Unframed, an open-source library of accessible, themeable components that work in React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Astro or plain HTML.

This article is about why I chose web components, and about the problems that turned out to be harder (and more interesting) than I expected.

Why web components

Custom elements are part of the browser. A <uf-button> works anywhere HTML works, with no framework runtime, no build step and no lock-in. Shadow DOM keeps each component's styles from leaking out, and your page's styles from leaking in by accident.

Writing them by hand is tedious, so Unframed is built with Lit: reactive properties, efficient rendering, and around 5 KB of runtime.

<uf-input name="email" type="email" label="Email" required></uf-input>
<uf-button type="submit">Sign up</uf-button>

That part was easy. Making them feel like they belong in each framework was not.

Problem 1: forms have to just work

A component library lives or dies on its form controls. If <uf-input> doesn't submit with the form, doesn't validate, or doesn't reset, nobody will use it.

Native inputs inside a shadow root are invisible to the surrounding <form>. The fix is ElementInternals: every Unframed form control is form-associated, so it shows up in FormData, takes part in native validation (required, pattern, min…), resets with the form, and is disabled by a disabled <fieldset>, just like a native input.

The surprising detail was timing. Lit batches updates, but forms read values synchronously: input.value = 'x'; form.requestSubmit() must see the new value immediately. So form-related properties update at once, while everything else keeps Lit's batching.

Then each framework has its own form system. Vue has v-model, Angular has ngModel and reactive forms. Unframed ships framework packages that wire these up, so in Vue you write <UfInput v-model="email" /> and in Angular <uf-input formControlName="email" />, with full type checking.

Problem 2: one source of truth for four frameworks

I didn’t want to hand-write React, Vue and Angular wrappers for every component. They would drift, exactly the problem I was trying to solve.

Instead, everything is generated from the Custom Elements Manifest, a JSON description of every component’s attributes, properties, events, slots and CSS parts, produced from the source code and its comments. From that single file, the build generates:

  • typed React components, with camelCase event handlers (onUfHide);
  • Vue components with typed props and v-model;
  • Angular standalone components and form directives, one entry point per component so bundles only include what you use;
  • the API tables in the docs, the Storybook controls, and a skill that teaches AI coding assistants how to use the library.

The build fails if a public property has no description, so the docs can’t fall behind the code.

Problem 3: server-side rendering

Web components and SSR have a reputation for not getting along, so I tested Unframed in real Next.js, Nuxt and Angular SSR apps instead of assuming. That turned up real bugs:

  • Next.js server components can’t use React hooks, so the React wrappers broke the build until I marked them as client components.
  • The server HTML was missing attributes. The React wrappers set props as properties, which only happens in the browser. So tabs rendered on the server didn’t know which panel was which, and showed all of them. The wrappers now write their attributes into the server HTML.
  • Raw content flashed before the JavaScript loaded: a closed dialog’s text, a menu’s items. A few lines of CSS for undefined elements now keep components invisible but in place until they’re ready.

Now every build checks that every component imports safely on a server.

Problem 4: accessibility you can trust

“Accessible” is easy to claim. I wanted it to be checked. Every component follows the matching WAI-ARIA pattern (arrow keys in tabs, menus, radio groups and the calendar, Escape to close, focus returning where it was), and every component’s tests run axe-core in a real browser, including popups and dialogs while they’re open.

Some of the most useful fixes came from these tests: a combobox whose empty list broke an ARIA rule, a code example’s copy button that didn’t belong inside a tab list. Small things that are easy to miss without automated checks.

What you get

  • The everyday components: buttons, inputs, select and combobox, date picker and date range picker, file upload, slider, dialog and drawer, tabs, table with sorting, pagination, toasts and more.
  • Theming with CSS custom properties and design tokens, light and dark mode, and a theme generator that checks the contrast of your colors.
  • Built-in translations for Italian, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese, following the page’s lang.
  • Packages for React, Vue and Angular, or plain HTML from a CDN.
  • A CLI to copy components into your project if you’d rather own the code.

The documentation site is built with the library itself, so every example on it is the real thing.

What’s next

Unframed is still 0.x: the API may change before 1.0, and I’m sure there are use cases I haven’t thought of. That’s exactly why I’m sharing it now. If you work on a design system, maintain apps in more than one framework, or just want to try web components in a real project, I’d love your feedback.

  • Docs: https://p-db.github.io/unframed-ui/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/P-DB/unframed-ui
  • npm: npm install @unframed/react @unframed/tokens (or /vue, /angular, /core)

If you try it, let me know what breaks. That’s the most useful thing you can tell me.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: RECORDE que não é RECORDE mas é RECORDE na MEIA de VALÊNCIA
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Recordes que não são recordes na Meia de Valência, novos detalhes sobre o doping de Peres Jepchirchir e um entregador que quase atrapalha a Maratona de Frankfurt. Confira também o desempenho dos brasileiros e a polêmica do gel de lactato.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Segunda-feira | 26 de outubro de 2026

A Meia Maratona de Valência, conhecida por ser extremamente rápida, teve dois recordes curiosos neste fim de semana. São recordes que, tecnicamente, não podem ser considerados, mas, ao mesmo tempo, são. Vamos explicar.

O espanhol Rodgrigue Kwizera venceu a prova com 58:03, estabelecendo o novo recorde espanhol. O curioso é que esse tempo é mais rápido que o recorde europeu (58:06, de Andreas Almgren), mas não pode ser validado como tal. Kwizera nasceu no Burundi e, apesar de ter se tornado cidadão espanhol, ainda está em um período de “quarentena” de transição de nacionalidade, o que o impede de competir em campeonatos mundiais e ter seu recorde validado a nível continental. No entanto, a federação espanhola reconhece a marca como recorde nacional.

Outro caso foi o do americano Yaseen Abdalla, que correu para 59:12, tempo mais rápido que o recorde americano de 59:17, de Conner Mantz. Contudo, Abdalla decidiu representar o Sudão, país de seus pais. Portanto, o recorde é validado como sudanês, mas não como americano.

Confira os resultados:

A polêmica do gel de lactato antes da prova

Um vídeo da marca de suplementos Santa Madre mostrou seus atletas patrocinados, incluindo os vencedores da Meia de Valência, consumindo gel de lactato antes da largada. A prática chamou a atenção porque vai contra alguns estudos que sugerem que o benefício desse tipo de gel ocorreria apenas no final da prova. A cena indica que talvez a ciência por trás do gel de lactato precise ser mais estudada, já que os atletas de elite estão adotando uma estratégia de uso pré-competição.

Brasileiros na Meia de Valência

Diversos brasileiros também se destacaram na rapidíssima prova espanhola. Brendon Bressan foi o melhor entre os homens, enquanto Bianca de Freitas liderou entre as mulheres. Confira o top 5:

Última etapa do ASICS Run Challenge em Floripa

O circuito ASICS Run Challenge, que tem parceria com o Corrida no Ar, está chegando à sua etapa final. Depois de passar por Belo Horizonte, Brasília, Fortaleza, Salvador e Recife, a última prova acontecerá em Florianópolis no dia 8 de novembro. As distâncias são de 4, 7 e 15 km, em provas com o excelente padrão da Vega, mesma organizadora da ASICS Golden Run. Se você quiser participar, aproveite os 10% de desconto usando o cupom CORRIDANOAR10.

Novos detalhes sobre o doping de Peres Jepchirchir

Surgiram novos e surpreendentes detalhes sobre o caso de doping da campeã olímpica Peres Jepchirchir. Segundo uma matéria exclusiva do site LetsRun, que conversou com o agente da atleta, Gianni Demadonna, o exame antidoping que testou positivo para EPO foi realizado seis semanas antes da Maratona de Sydney, e não na véspera da viagem, como se imaginava. Isso sugere que ela acreditava que a substância já teria saído de seu organismo.

Além disso, foi revelado que os agentes da Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) enfrentaram um impasse de duas horas na casa da atleta no Quênia. O segurança não permitia a entrada, e os agentes precisaram ligar para Demadonna. O agente, então, ligou para Jepchirchir e avisou: “Se você não abrir a porta, será suspensa por dois anos”. Só então ela permitiu a coleta. Demadonna se disse chocado, afirmando que a atleta nunca teve problemas com doping e especula que a lesão que a tirou de Londres e a pressão de ver outras atletas correndo rápido possam tê-la influenciado.

Entregador quase estraga a Maratona de Frankfurt

Na Maratona de Frankfurt, o atleta alemão Amanal Petros, que terminou em segundo lugar, quase teve sua prova arruinada por um entregador de bicicleta. Perto da linha de chegada, o ciclista cruzou o percurso e quase causou uma colisão com o corredor. Felizmente, Petros conseguiu desviar e completar a prova sem maiores problemas.

Resultados e brasileiros na Maratona de Frankfurt

A prova teve vitória do etíope Jiksa Tolosa com 2:05:26. Amanal Petros foi o segundo, com 2:05:46, e o queniano Bernard Biwott Kipkurui fechou o pódio com 2:06:23. No feminino, a vencedora foi Zenebe Imer Worku, da Etiópia, com 2:19:45, seguida pela alemã Bianca Dörfel (2:20:46) e pela também etíope Beriha Gebrehiwot (2:22:46).
